title: No prying
hookLine: nothing is more wretched than going round prying into others' souls (Meditations 2.13)

cards: It's eleven at night, and you're four years deep into the vacation photos of someone you don't even like.
Or you're piecing together, from a coworker's tone and a calendar invite, exactly what's going on between those two. Nobody asked you to. It's not useful.
It doesn't even feel good. And yet it's oddly hard to stop. A few days ago Marcus said to watch your own mind.
Today he goes further, and he doesn't soften it.

teach.b: Nothing is more wretched, Marcus says, than a person who goes round and round everything, digging into the things beneath the earth, as the poet says, and trying to guess what's in the minds of the people around them.
Wretched is a big word, and he means it. The prying mind is busy, restless and never full. Second, the poet.
The phrase about the things beneath the earth comes from the Greek poet Pindar. Plato once borrowed it to describe a philosopher whose mind ranges over everything.
Marcus turns it around: that endless searching, pointed at other people's business, is a misery, not a virtue. Third, what's enough.
It's enough, he says, to attend to the guiding spirit within you, and to serve it sincerely, keeping it clean of turmoil, of carelessness, and of resentment toward gods and people.
One inner life to look after is a full-time job. Fourth, how to see others.
When you do look at people, Marcus says, look with affection, because they're your kin.

Sometimes, even, with a kind of pity, when they don't know good from bad, which he calls a blindness no smaller than not telling black from white. Notice the order. Not suspicion, not curiosity, not judgment.
Affection first. Pity, when it's called for. Prying has no place in that list.
Not my business isn't coldness. It's giving people the privacy you'd want, and giving yourself back the evening.

how: Readers who take this entry to heart often cut back on gossip and checking up on others, and turn that attention to their own character instead.

o: never ask anyone a question about their life
keep your own secrets locked away from others
don't dig into others' lives; tend your own spirit

s: Marcus calls endless curiosity about others a virtue
he calls the person who pries into others' minds wretched.
Marcus borrows a phrase from the poet Pindar
'the things beneath the earth', which Plato had also used.
Marcus says to look on other people with suspicion
with affection, as kin, and sometimes with pity.

games.q: you notice two coworkers acting strangely, and you could piece together what's going on. what does Meditations 2.13 suggest?
o: let it be, tend your own mind, and treat them kindly.
games.why: it's enough to attend to the spirit within, Marcus says, and to see others with affection, not to pry.

practice: Think of one place your curiosity goes where it isn't needed, a profile you check, a rumor you follow, and picture closing that door gently and turning back toward your own inner room.
Then think of the person you were prying into, and send them one plain thought of goodwill.

wordCard.voice: No prying. Marcus says nothing is more wretched than digging into other people's minds; tend your own inner spirit, and see others with affection. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a guiding spirit. Marcus's word for the divine part within each person, to be tended and revered.

carryVoice: Your line: not my business. Affection first, and pity when it's called for. That's day five hundred thirty-seven.
